articles.description: In a significant step towards addressing India’s dual burden of malnutrition, The George Institute for Global Health, India, in collaboration with Rutgers University and other global partners, has developed a set of innovative tools designed to map and better understand the country’s diverse and evolving food environments. The new toolkit, published in Current Developments in Nutrition, was co-authored by Dr Suparna Ghosh-Jerath from The George Institute and led by Dr Shauna Downs from Rutgers School of Public Health. The initiative aims to generate critical data on food access, availability, affordability, and quality across various Indian settings. Despite shifts towards market-based diets, India continues to struggle with widespread nutrient deficiencies, referred to as "hidden hunger", and an alarming rise in non-communicable diseases like diabetes and hypertension. The NFHS-5 survey has highlighted staggering rates of anaemia among women and children, pointing to an urgent need for improved diet diversity and nutritional adequacy. The newly developed Food Environment Toolbox includes seven practical tools, such as participatory mapping, seasonal food availability calendars, and vendor assessments. These were piloted in rural, peri-urban, and urban settings in India and Cambodia to ensure their relevance and adaptability across diverse environments.“Most existing tools are built for high-income countries and don’t reflect the complexity of LMIC food systems,” said Dr Suparna Ghosh-Jerath. “Our toolbox captures the informal and dynamic nature of food environments in India and similar nations.”Dr Shauna Downs added, “These tools are easy to implement and were well-received in the field. For instance, seasonal food calendars worked best in rural settings, while vendor assessments suited open markets better than supermarkets.”The toolbox holds promise for enhancing major nutrition programs like POSHAN Abhiyaan, ICDS, Mid-Day Meal Scheme, and the Public Distribution System. It urges a shift in focus—from mere calorie sufficiency to nutrient adequacy—ensuring government schemes are responsive to local food environments and dietary practices. Experts now advocate for double-duty nutrition policies—those that tackle both undernutrition and diet-related diseases—driven by data, contextual understanding, and inclusive strategies. As India strives to meet its public health goals, these practical, scalable tools may play a crucial role in reshaping national nutrition strategies, ultimately improving health outcomes and food security for millions.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace faces its biggest test over Gaza
articles.description: The Board of Peace, set up under US President Donald Trump's initiative, is approaching a crucial stage. Seen as an important effort to end the Gaza conflict and bring lasting peace to the Palestinian, the question now is: can it deliver on the ground? Its objectives included ending hostilities, moving Gaza away from Hamas rule, ensuring the withdrawal of Israeli forces and beginning reconstruction. A year back, the Board was formally launched with Trump as its chairman. The initiative received a lot of international backing through UN Security Council Resolution 2803. Its February 19 meeting in Washington further raised expectations, with several countries announcing financial commitments for Gaza's reconstruction. There has been some progress. The October 2025 ceasefire, the return of all hostages, the release of Palestinian prisoners and the expansion of humanitarian assistance were important developments. The Board's May 2026 report to the Security Council also referred to the establishment of an international organisation, a 28-member National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), preparations for an International Stabilisation Force (ISF) and reconstruction pledges amounting to $17 billion. Five countries: Albania, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kosovo and Morocco expressed their intention to contribute troops to the proposed stabilisation force. A pre-deployment assessment was also completed in April. These developments suggest that the Board has moved forward positively and has started putting an institutional structure in place. However, the Board's next phase of the peace plan looks somewhat stranded. Hamas and other Palestinian groups are expected to surrender civilian governance and security responsibilities to the NCAG. The proposed international force would monitor the ceasefire, support humanitarian deliveries and help train Palestinian police. Israel, meanwhile, is expected to withdraw in stages, while the process of disarming armed groups would be monitored. Reconstruction is also expected to begin under the supervision of the Board and the Palestinian technocratic administration. Israel and Hamas, the two major players in the conflict were supposed to cooperate but it is not happening. Scattered violence in Gaza continues. Civilians’ deaths continue. Hospitals remain under threat and displaced families cannot return to their homes. The recent Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis on November 11, which killed at least six people, including a doctor and a 13-year-old boy, once again exposed the fragile situation. The Israeli military said it had targeted a Hamas commander and militants allegedly operating from the hospital. Hamas denied using the hospital complex for military purposes. The Board deplored the civilian casualties and called on Israel and Hamas to honour their commitments under the peace plan. It also urged all parties to protect civilians and provide the necessary authority and operational space for establishing secure, demilitarised medical facilities. Earlier, the Board had criticised Israel's response to flooding in Gaza and called for the entry of shelter, sanitation, drainage and winter supplies. Political observers feel that issuing statements is not enough. The real question is whether the Board can prevent further violence and ensure that humanitarian assistance reaches those who need it. According to the UN's November 5 humanitarian situation report, 1,593 Palestinians had been reported killed and 5,748 injured since the ceasefire agreement. Nearly two million Palestinians remain displaced, with homes, hospitals and essential infrastructure destroyed. For ordinary Palestinians, the success of the Board will be judged by whether they can live without fear, get medical treatment, receive food and shelter and return to a normal life. If these basic conditions cannot be ensured, the Board's claims of progress will always be questioned. Political commentators observe that the main problem is not administrative but political. Israel insists that Hamas must be disarmed before reconstruction can proceed. Hamas, on the other hand, is reluctant to surrender its weapons and political influence without clear guarantees about Palestinian rights, Israeli withdrawal and the future governance of Gaza. There is a roadmap. But who will ensure that both sides honour their commitments? The proposed International Stabilisation Force is central to the entire arrangement. Its success will depend on how many countries contribute troops, what powers the force is given, and whether it can operate effectively without being drawn into another confrontation. Civilians living there must feel that they are regaining control over their lives and institutions. There are also questions about the Board's own structure. It raises concerns about accountability and continuity. The Board has the endorsement of the UN Security Council for its role in Gaza, but it is not a replacement for the United Nations. It does not have the same universal authority or enforcement powers as the Security Council. Its strength depends on political influence, financial support and the willingness of participating countries to cooperate. The Board's credibility will depend on how it is viewed by Palestinians, Israel and the wider international community. For Palestinians, the immediate priorities are security, food, shelter, functioning hospitals and schools. For Israel, the priority is a guarantee that Hamas will not rebuild its military capabilities. For the international community, the question is whether the Board can function as an impartial peace mechanism or will remain largely an extension of American foreign policy. Some European countries have also expressed reservations about its mandate and its relationship with existing UN institutions. France and other critics have stressed that its activities should remain focused on Gaza. The Board will also have to ensure transparency in the use of reconstruction funds. Financial pledges running into billions of dollars will mean little unless the money reaches Gaza and produces visible improvements in people's lives. The Board no doubt has provided a diplomatic framework, secured financial commitments and established administrative arrangements. But it would be premature to describe it as a successful peace mechanism. It has made progress in setting up the structure, but its ability to enforce decisions remains still at a distance. Last week's US midterm election results have introduced an important political factor. The Democrats have secured control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. This may be a major setback for Trump, who began his second term with Republicans controlling both chambers. The new Congress will take office on January 3, 2027. But the election outcome has already changed the political atmosphere in Washington. For the Board of Peace, this could have consequences. A Democratic-controlled Congress is likely to scrutinise the administration's financial commitments, reconstruction spending and wider West Asia policy more closely. It may seek answers about the Board's functioning. This may put additional pressure on Trump to demonstrate that his peace initiative is delivering results. However, the election results do not mean the Board will automatically cease to function. Foreign policy and diplomatic negotiations remain largely within the authority of the President and the executive branch. Trump will continue as chairman of the Board, and the new Congress cannot simply remove him from that position. However, congressional control matters. Funding, oversight and political pressure can influence the extent of American support for the initiative. Domestic political battles could divert his attention and reduce the personal involvement that has so far driven the Board. The real test will be whether he treats the initiative as a lasting international commitment or primarily as an achievement associated with his presidency. The coming months are crucial and will determine whether the Board can turn its plans into reality. Without accountability, the ceasefire will remain vulnerable to repeated breakdowns. For India, developments in Gaza are important for several reasons. Stability in West Asia is closely linked to India's energy security, trade and the safety of millions of Indians living and working in the region. New Delhi has consistently supported a negotiated two-state solution and would want Gaza's reconstruction to take place through a credible process. Ultimately, the Board faces three difficult questions. Can it persuade Israel to exercise restraint and withdraw in accordance with an agreed framework? Can it ensure that Hamas gives up its armed and governing role? And can it provide Palestinians with a functioning administration and a genuine political future? The Board is yet to prove that it can guarantee peace. It has moved beyond announcements and created an institutional framework. However, continuing violence, the humanitarian crisis and uncertainty over the international force show how far it remains from achieving its objectives. The Board still has an opportunity to prove that it can make a difference. But its credibility will not be decided in Washington or at international conferences. It will be judged at ground zero, in Gaza's hospitals, on its damaged streets and among the families waiting to return to their homes. Authour is National Editor, Greater Kashmir
